political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.

These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

memory.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering
strands.focus: Family, religious and class contexts organize recollection; a collective framework is not proof of one identical group memory.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); English selections (1992)

strands.title: Sites of memory and historical reconstruction
strands.focus: Sites combine material, symbolic and functional dimensions, extending beyond monuments alone.

strands.title: Habit, bodies and ceremony
strands.focus: Remembering includes bodily competence, not only recalled propositions or pictures.

strands.title: Communication and cultural objectivation
strands.focus: Everyday recollection and durable cultural forms operate differently; Assmann revises rather than merely repeats Halbwachs.

strands.title: Media and uses of cultural memory
strands.focus: Writing, images and monuments organize what can be stored and recalled.

strands.title: Mourning and cultural continuities after war
strands.focus: Traditional and modern forms overlap in Great War mourning; this is not a template for every subsequent catastrophe.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

strands.title: Holocaust memorials and their contexts
strands.focus: Memorial forms and meanings vary across places and institutions.

strands.title: Popular practices of historical knowledge
strands.focus: Family research, images and reenactment make historical work visible outside professional writing.

strands.title: Life histories, gender and subjectivity
strands.focus: Fascist everyday life and feminist psychoanalytic inquiry are distinct routes into interpreted recollection.

strands.title: Archival authority, access and inscription
strands.focus: Combe’s inquiry into access supplies a named resource to Derrida. His account differentiates archives from spontaneous memory and examines institutional authority and technical inscription. From the archival profession, Schwartz and Cook called archives 'active sites where social power is negotiated' whose appraisal and access shape collective memory (2002, abstract); the wider readership is on the entry archival_turn.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public memory
strands.focus: Hayden’s collaborative practice links historical interpretation to lived places.

strands.title: Traditions in contact and conflict
strands.focus: Halbwachs explains revisions of collective remembering through contact with other groups and their traditions; social frameworks are not an assurance of a unanimous or unchanging past.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925), final concluding subsection

strands.title: Memorial production and public disagreement
strands.focus: Young’s Saarbrücken account follows a covert art project into public controversy and political recognition. His interpretation makes the memorial’s production and reception part of its meaning.
strands.works: Germany’s vanishing Holocaust monuments (1994), adapted extract

strands.title: Argentina: rights, remembrance and generations
strands.focus: Jelin examines competing public memories and tensions within human-rights activism. Her conclusion questions both political forgetting and repetition that prevents younger generations from reinterpreting the past.
strands.works: The Politics of Memory (1994), selected sections

strands.title: Vichy’s afterlife and historical inquiry
strands.focus: Rousso distinguishes memory as an object of research, as a preliminary examination of inherited representations, and as a way to extend an event’s historical study into its aftermath.
strands.works: Pour une histoire de la mémoire collective (1991), 163–166

strands.focus: Yerushalmi’s prologue asks why concern with historical meaning and remembrance need not give professional historical writing the central role. This is a situated historical question, not a timeless definition of Jewish people.

strands.title: Resources for studying forgetting
strands.focus: Jelin’s 1994 analysis explicitly draws on Yerushalmi’s transmission argument and Loraux’s treatment of amnesty and mourning. Their Spanish 1989 essays are distinct from Zakhor.
strands.works: Usos del olvido essays (1989), as used by Jelin (1994)

consumption.label: Consumption & material culture
consumption.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.

Additional readings: Douglas and Isherwood, The World of Goods (1979); Kopytoff on cultural biography (1986); de Vries on industrious change (1994); de Grazia and Furlough, The Sex of Things (1996). Maxine Berg and Helen Clifford, eds.: Consumers and Luxury (1999).

consumption.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.

strands.title: Relics and changing value
strands.focus: Geary follows transfers and renewed authentication of relics. Their careers may change how communities value them; price equivalences and the relative frequency of different transfers remain uncertain.

strands.title: Specific historical uses of theory
strands.focus: Vickery explicitly uses Bourdieu and Douglas/Isherwood; Geary cites Kopytoff. These establish particular uses with different evidence and questions, without proving uniform reception across consumption history.
